newsitem.title: USA: US Clinton, Republican wins seen as best bond brew.
newsitem.headline: US Clinton, Republican wins seen as best bond brew.

text.p: The re-election triumph of President Bill Clinton and the continued control of the U.S. Congress by Republicans could spur further gains in the U.S. bond market, analysts said.

"The best outcome for the financial markets is Clinton in the White House and Republicans in the Congress," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "With the Republicans in the Congress, you presumably get tight control over spending, no Clinton mandate, a fiscal policy that would be more restrained than it might be otherwise."

Moran said a victory for Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole, combined with a Republican Congress, might have hurt the markets because the 15-percent tax cut Dole promised during his campaign could have widened the budget deficit.

"As rocky as the budget process was this past year, in the end we got something that was favorable for the public," Moran said. "You had some spending cuts, but not the slash-and-burn cuts the Republicans might have pushed through on their own. You got the centrist fiscal policy that the public prefers and we should get something similar over the next two years."
Overseas, the dollar reacted favorably to news that the Republicans were going to retain their hold on the Senate, firming to 114 yen in midday trade in Tokyo.
"This is stasis for fiscal policy," said David Garrow, a Pulitzer-prize winning historian. "No one has the initiative here. There's certainly no mandate for Clinton."
Margaret Patel, managing director and portfolio manager of Greenwich, Ct.-based Northstar Mutual Funds, agreed.
"The people spoke, but they didn't give a clear mandate to one party or the other," said Patel.
The public has come to believe that a balanced federal budget is a desirable goal, said Patel.

"The track we're on for deficit reduction is really just too strong and is not going to be changed," she said. "There clearly is no will to move away from deficit reduction as a fiscal goal for the country."

Although traders and investors feel upbeat about the preservation of the political status quo in the 1996 U.S. election, the market is also benefitting from longer-term macroeconomic trends, analysts said.

"The economic forces in play -- which really come down to low inflation here and worldwide -- are too big to be influenced in the near term by one political party or by one election or another," said Patel.
Raymond Worseck, chief economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc, agreed.

"The bond market is much more a creature of financial and economic pressures," he said. "Bond yields have been coming down in Germany and Japan. We had (U.S. economic) numbers last week that showed that wage pressures and inflation were less than expected. There's been weakness in commodity prices."
Worseck said the bond market showed some euphoria in Tuesday's trading in anticipation of the election outcome, but that it would soon refocus on "more traditional influences."

"We'll get some good-feelings spillover on Wednesday," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi. "The Republicans held the Congress and Clinton kept the Presidency. The market wants to go higher."

Rupkey said if House Speaker Newt Gingrich were to say that he was willing to work together with the Administration to get a balanced budget by 2002, the market could start to try to move higher on that.

"People are no longer running for re-election so they can hopefully get back to the business of balancing the budget," said Rupkey. "Anything suggesting that we could go to zero on the budget deficit is very, very good for bonds."
